summary: Defines the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP), by which MPLS routers tell each other what labels they use so traffic can be forwarded along normally routed paths. It is a Draft Standard.

eli5.summary: Routers agree on short sticker labels for packages so they pass along faster.

questions: how do mpls routers exchange labels
how do ldp peers establish a session
subtitle: How MPLS routers agree on the labels they stick on packets, so traffic can follow normally routed paths.

tldr.problem: In MPLS, two neighboring Label Switching Routers (LSRs) must agree on what each label means before they can forward traffic by label. They need a standard way to tell each other.
tldr.mechanism: LDP has routers find each other with UDP Hello messages, open a TCP session, negotiate parameters, and then exchange label mappings that tie a Forwarding Equivalence Class (a set of packets, such as an address prefix) to a label.
tldr.outcome: This document is a Draft Standard that replaces RFC 3036 and has since been updated by RFC 6720, RFC 6790, RFC 7358 and RFC 7552. It is the base specification of LDP.

today: RFC 5036 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 3036. It has been updated by RFC 6720, RFC 6790, RFC 7358 and RFC 7552.

sections.title: What LDP Is For
sections.content:
The MPLS architecture (RFC 3031) says that two Label Switching Routers must agree on the meaning of the labels used to forward traffic between and through them. A label distribution protocol is the set of procedures by which one LSR tells another about the label bindings it has made. The Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) is one such protocol, defined to support MPLS forwarding along normally routed paths.

LDP is the set of procedures and messages by which LSRs establish Label Switched Paths (LSPs) through a network, mapping network-layer routing information directly to data-link layer switched paths. An LSP may end at a directly attached neighbor, which is comparable to IP hop-by-hop forwarding, or at a network egress node. The protocol was first published as RFC 3036 in January 2001, and this document replaces it.

Two LSRs that exchange label and FEC mapping information are LDP peers, and there is an LDP session between them. One session lets each peer learn the other's mappings, so the protocol is bidirectional.

LDP messages fall into four categories: discovery messages that announce an LSR's presence, session messages that set up and tear down sessions, advertisement messages that create, change and delete label mappings, and notification messages that carry advisory and error information.
sections.eli5: Neighboring routers need to speak the same sticker language. LDP is the way they teach each other what each sticker means, and each pair of neighbors keeps a chat going to do it.

sections.title: FECs, Label Spaces and LDP Identifiers
sections.content:
LDP associates a Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) with each LSP. The FEC says which packets are mapped to that LSP. It is made of one or more FEC elements, and this specification defines a single kind, the Address Prefix FEC element, a prefix of any length from 0 to a full address. A packet matches an LSP when the packet's destination address begins with the LSP's prefix.

If a packet matches several LSPs, it is mapped to the one whose matching prefix is longest. If it is known that a packet must cross a particular egress router and an LSP exists for that router's /32 address, the packet is mapped to that LSP.

A label space is either per interface (for example ATM VCIs or Frame Relay DLCIs used as labels) or per platform (labels shared across interfaces). An LDP Identifier is a six octet value naming one label space of an LSR. The first four octets identify the LSR and must be globally unique, such as a 32-bit router Id. The last two octets name the label space and are both zero for a platform-wide label space. It is printed as <LSR Id> : <label space id>, for example lsr171:0.

An LSR that advertises more than one label space to a peer uses a separate LDP session, and so a separate TCP connection, for each one.
sections.eli5: A FEC is a rule like 'all parcels going to this neighborhood get the same sticker'. A label space is the sticker book a router uses, and its LDP Identifier is the name on the cover.

sections.title: Discovery and Session Setup
sections.content:
Routers find peers by discovery, so nobody has to configure each neighbor by hand. In Basic Discovery, an LSR periodically sends LDP Link Hellos as UDP packets to the well-known LDP port at the 'all routers on this subnet' multicast group. Each Hello carries the LDP Identifier of the label space the sender wants to use on that interface. In Extended Discovery, an LSR sends Targeted Hellos to a specific address, which allows sessions between LSRs that are not directly connected. Targeted discovery is asymmetric: the target decides whether to respond.

Receiving a Hello creates a Hello adjacency. Each adjacency has a hold timer, and if no matching Hello arrives before it expires, the adjacency is deleted. When the last adjacency for a session is deleted, the LSR ends the session. The Hello hold time is negotiated as the minimum of the two proposals; a value of 0 means the default of 15 seconds for Link Hellos and 45 seconds for Targeted Hellos, and 0xffff means infinite.

Hellos trigger session establishment in two steps. First comes the TCP connection. Each LSR works out the transport addresses for both ends, either from the Transport Address TLV in the Hello or from the Hello's source address. It then compares them as unsigned integers: the LSR with the higher address plays the active role and connects to the well-known LDP port, and the other waits as the passive peer. Both the UDP port for Hellos and the TCP port for sessions are 646.

Second comes initialization: the active LSR sends an Initialization message proposing session parameters such as the protocol version, label distribution method and timer values. The passive LSR matches the LDP Identifier in that message to a Hello adjacency, and replies with its own Initialization message and a KeepAlive message if it accepts. The active LSR then sends a KeepAlive, and the session is operational once each side has received both an acceptable Initialization and a KeepAlive.

If the parameters are unacceptable, the receiver sends an error Notification and closes the TCP connection. To avoid an endless loop of rejections, an LSR MUST back off exponentially: the first retry after a rejected Initialization MUST be delayed no less than 15 seconds, and delays MUST grow to a maximum of no less than 2 minutes.

Once running, each LSR resets a KeepAlive timer whenever it receives any LDP PDU from the peer. It must send some PDU to the peer at least every KeepAlive period, and sends a KeepAlive message when it has nothing else to say. An LSR ends a session deliberately by sending a Shutdown message.
sections.eli5: Routers shout 'hello, I'm here!' to the neighborhood. When two hear each other, the one with the bigger address phones the other, they agree on the rules, and then they keep saying 'still here' so neither thinks the other has left.

sections.title: The Session Initialization State Machine
sections.content:
The RFC describes session negotiation as a state machine with five states: NON EXISTENT, INITIALIZED, OPENREC, OPENSENT and OPERATIONAL. A session starts at NON EXISTENT and moves to INITIALIZED when the TCP connection is established.

From INITIALIZED, the active LSR transmits an Initialization message and moves to OPENSENT. The passive LSR, on receiving an acceptable Initialization message, transmits its own Initialization and a KeepAlive and moves to OPENREC. An active LSR in OPENSENT that receives an acceptable Initialization sends a KeepAlive and moves to OPENREC. Receiving a KeepAlive in OPENREC makes the session OPERATIONAL.

In the three setup states, any other LDP message causes the LSR to transmit an error Notification (a NAK), close the transport connection, and return to NON EXISTENT. In OPERATIONAL, a Shutdown message or a timeout leads to a Shutdown message being sent, the connection closing and a return to NON EXISTENT; other messages leave the state unchanged. A Shutdown message is implemented as a Notification message whose Status TLV signals a fatal error.
sections.eli5: Setting up a call goes through steps: the line connects, one side says its rules, the other agrees, and finally both say 'okay, go'. If anyone says something unexpected before then, they hang up and start over.

sections.title: How Labels Are Handed Out
sections.content:
LDP supports two ways to hand out labels, and both can be used in the same network. In Downstream Unsolicited mode an LSR advertises a label binding to peers that have not asked for it. In Downstream on Demand mode it provides a binding only in answer to an explicit Label Request. Each interface is configured for one mode, and LSRs exchange their modes during initialization.

Label distribution control decides when mappings may be sent. With independent control, each LSR may advertise mappings any time it likes, so an upstream label can be advertised before a downstream label has been received. With ordered control, an LSR may send a mapping for a FEC only if it already has one from the FEC's next hop or is itself the egress for that FEC.

Label retention decides what an LSR does with mappings from neighbors that are not the next hop. Conservative retention keeps only labels that will be used for forwarding, which saves label space (for instance in an ATM switch) but means a new label must be obtained if routing changes the next hop. Liberal retention keeps every mapping received, which reacts quickly to routing changes but stores unneeded labels.

LSRs keep learned labels in a Label Information Base. To translate between a peer's LDP Identifier and its addresses, they advertise addresses with Address messages and withdraw them with Address Withdraw messages.

Loop detection is a configurable option. Path Vector TLVs list the LSRs a message has traversed, and Hop Count TLVs count them. An LSR that sees its own Id in a Path Vector, or a count at the configured maximum, treats the message as having looped and sends a Loop Detected Notification. Appendix A is the authoritative description of label distribution procedures; if it conflicts with text elsewhere, Appendix A wins.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a router hands out stickers before anyone asks, and sometimes only when asked. Some routers keep every sticker they are given just in case, and others keep only the ones they need.

sections.title: PDUs, TLVs and Messages
sections.content:
Every LDP PDU is an LDP header followed by one or more messages. The header holds a two octet Version (this document specifies version 1), a two octet PDU Length and the six octet LDP Identifier of the sender's label space. Before a session's maximum PDU length is negotiated, it is 4096 bytes.

Much of the information is encoded as Type-Length-Value (TLV) objects: a 2 octet field with 14 bits of Type and two behavior bits, then a 2 octet Length, then the Value. If the U bit is clear and an LSR does not recognize a TLV, it returns a notification and ignores the whole message; if U is set, the TLV is silently ignored. The F bit says whether an unknown TLV is forwarded with the message, so setting both lets a TLV pass as opaque data through nodes that do not understand it. TLVs can be nested.

All messages share one layout: a U bit, a Message Type, a Message Length, a 32-bit Message ID, then mandatory and optional parameters. The Message ID lets Notifications refer to the message they concern. A Label Mapping message carries a FEC TLV and a Label TLV, and it MUST include the Label Request Message ID parameter when answering a Label Request.

The Hello message carries a Common Hello Parameters TLV with the hold time, a T bit marking a Targeted Hello and an R bit asking the receiver to send Targeted Hellos back. The document also reserves vendor-private and experimental ranges for messages and TLVs, so extensions can be added.
sections.eli5: Every note LDP sends has a little envelope with who it is from, and inside are labeled boxes. A box says what kind it is and how big it is, so a router that does not know a box can skip it or complain.

sections.title: Security: Spoofing, Privacy and Denial of Service
sections.content:
The RFC names two spoofing targets. UDP discovery can be attacked because a spoofed Hello with a small hold time can make an existing adjacency time out and end its session. Suggested defenses are accepting Basic Hellos only on interfaces to trusted directly connected LSRs, ignoring Basic Hellos not addressed to the All Routers multicast group, and filtering Extended Hellos with access lists. TCP session traffic is protected by the TCP MD5 Signature Option for authenticity and integrity. The RFC notes that RFC 2385 says MD5 is considered by some to be too weak, and that LDP could move to a stronger TCP digest option if one were defined and deployed.

On privacy, LDP provides no mechanism to protect the privacy of label distribution. The RFC argues that its authenticity and integrity protection gives a level of security at least as good as, though no better than, that of the routing protocols themselves. Label spoofing is avoided only by making sure labeled packets are labeled by trusted LSRs using properly learned labels.

For denial of service, the well-known UDP discovery port and TCP session port are the two targets. Extended Hellos are potentially the more serious threat. An LSR SHOULD avoid promiscuous TCP listens and use only listens specific to discovered peers, and access lists at the edge of an MPLS cloud can protect interior LSRs.
sections.eli5: Someone could pretend to be a neighbor or flood a router with fake hellos. Routers defend by only listening to neighbors they trust and by signing their messages with a secret.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 3036
sections.content:
This document is a revision of RFC 3036. Among the listed changes, it removes the Host Address FEC because no implementation used it, splits the references into normative and informative, replaces a reference to BGP with RFC 4271, clarifies the use of the F-bit, and adds an option to allow split horizon with Ordered Control. It also explains the security threat posed by Hello spoofing and clarifies how to interoperate when sending vendor-private TLVs and messages.

The RFC also lists topics left for future study, including Class of Service, multicast, multipath label switching and basic peer discovery on non-broadcast multi-access media.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the rulebook. The authors fixed unclear parts, removed a rule nobody used, and listed things for later.
